name: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy
heroTitle: Describe the difference you want to notice.
summary: Solution-focused therapy explores a preferred future, useful exceptions, and small signs of change. See how its questions differ from forced optimism or advice to simply try harder.
panelTitle: A goal becomes useful when it becomes recognizable.
panelParagraphs: Less stress is a hope. Being able to finish work and stay present at dinner is a picture you can explore, refine, and review.

model.title: A preferred future gives the conversation direction.
paragraphs: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy emphasizes what a person wants to be different, what is already helping, and how useful changes might become more possible. Rather than requiring an exhaustive explanation of a problem before work can begin, it explores a concrete picture of improvement.

The approach pays attention to exceptions: times when the difficulty was less intense or a desired response was already possible. Exceptions are not evidence that the problem is imaginary. They are information about circumstances, supports, skills, or choices that may matter.

Brief describes a focus on purposeful, efficient work, not a guarantee of a fixed number of appointments. Some difficulties require more extensive assessment, specialized treatment, or practical support. A solution-focused conversation should not bypass those needs or turn structural barriers into a lack of motivation.

panel.title: Small does not mean trivial.
paragraphs: A manageable difference can show what matters. It is not automatically sufficient for a major problem, but it can be a useful place to begin learning.

example.title: A calmer morning starts with a specific picture.
example.intro: A fictional example about one person's difficult start to the workday.

items.title: The broad wish
paragraphs: Lee wants mornings to be less chaotic. Asked what would be different, they describe finding their belongings, leaving without an argument, and having a few quiet minutes before work.

items.title: The exception
paragraphs: There was one easier morning the previous week. A family member handled an errand, and Lee had prepared an important item the night before. It was not simply a more positive attitude.

items.title: The small next difference
paragraphs: The conversation identifies which conditions might be repeatable and which require help. The first experiment is sized to Lee's actual responsibilities rather than an idealized routine.

reveal.title: Why look closely at the easier morning?
paragraphs: The exception gives detail to a vague hope. Perhaps cooperation mattered more than personal organization, or the critical change was having fewer simultaneous demands. A therapist can help explore the ingredients without assuming that one successful day supplies a universal solution.

Lee might describe the next step as having one less rushed moment, not achieving a perfect morning. Reviewing what happened can reveal whether the plan was useful or whether a different barrier needs attention. The example illustrates inquiry, not prescribed homework.

toolsTitle: Questions that look for direction and usable information.
toolsIntro: The method is collaborative. The therapist is not supposed to supply your preferred future for you.

tools.title: Preferred-future questions
tools.teaser: What would improvement look like in ordinary life?
paragraphs: A question may invite a detailed description of how a day, conversation, or decision would be different if therapy helped. Observable details turn a general wish into something that can be discussed.
The imagined future should remain connected to your values and circumstances, not a fantasy in which every external difficulty disappears.

tools.title: Exceptions and existing resources
tools.teaser: When has a useful difference already occurred?
paragraphs: The clinician may explore moments when the problem had less influence. What was different about the setting, support, timing, or response? The aim is to discover information, not prove that you should be able to reproduce the moment at will.
Sometimes a missing resource, rather than a missing skill, is the decisive difference.

tools.title: Scaling and coping questions
tools.teaser: Describe change without pretending a number explains everything.
paragraphs: A scale can open a conversation about where you are, what keeps things from being worse, and what a small improvement would look like. The number is a prompt, not a diagnosis or a validated outcome by itself.
Coping questions can recognize what has helped someone endure a difficult period without praising them into accepting an intolerable situation.

processTitle: From a broad hope to something worth trying.

process.title: Describe what would make therapy useful
paragraphs: The work begins with your own priorities. A goal can be revised when you discover that the original wording did not capture what mattered.

process.title: Look for useful differences
paragraphs: Explore exceptions, coping, relationships, and resources. Understanding how something helped is more useful than merely calling it a strength.

process.title: Consider a manageable step
paragraphs: An action or observation can be chosen collaboratively. It should account for available time, support, access, and energy.

process.title: Notice and review change
paragraphs: Later conversations examine what is different and whether it is meaningful. Lack of change is information for revising the plan, not proof of personal failure.

limitsTitle: A future focus should not erase the difficulty.

limits.title: Not forced positivity
paragraphs: You do not have to describe a painful situation as a blessing. Loss, inequity, illness, and exhaustion can remain real while you explore what support or improvement might be possible.

limits.title: Not a replacement for assessment
paragraphs: Risk, severe symptoms, or a specialized treatment need still require appropriate assessment. A useful question about change cannot establish diagnosis, safety, or the right level of care on its own.

questions.question: Does brief mean only a few sessions?
paragraphs: It does not promise a particular count. The intention is focused work responsive to your goals. Duration also depends on the presenting concerns, progress, available services, and whether a different treatment is needed.

questions.question: Will we ignore my history?
paragraphs: The approach emphasizes useful change and current resources, but relevant history can still matter. Explain when you need past experiences to be understood, and ask how that need fits the clinician's style.

questions.question: What if I cannot imagine things getting better?
paragraphs: That difficulty can be part of the conversation. A starting point might be describing what feels most urgent or what helps you get through a day. You should not be pushed to manufacture an optimistic answer.

questions.question: What if the problem is outside my control?
paragraphs: Then control itself needs to be distinguished from influence and support. A plan should not assume that individual effort can solve unsafe housing, another person's behavior, or inaccessible resources. Practical assistance or a different service may be important.

questions.question: How is this different from simply setting goals?
paragraphs: The work includes detailed exploration of the preferred future, exceptions, resources, and signs of change. It is a therapeutic conversation, not merely writing a target and being held accountable for achieving it.

questions.question: Can couples use this approach?
paragraphs: There are solution-focused applications with couples, but training and appropriateness need confirmation. A method that explores exceptions should never be used to minimize harm or pressure a partner to participate.
